events.name: Martyrs of Najran
events.summary: The Christian community of Najran was put to death under the Himyarite king Dhu Nuwas, an event remembered in Qur'an 85 and in church tradition.
events.context: Himyar in Yemen had adopted Judaism in the fifth century; Dhu Nuwas's persecution followed years of religious conflict between Himyar and the Christian kingdom of Aksum across the Red Sea.
events.significance: The persecution gave Aksum the occasion to invade Yemen, so the Red Sea corridor between Arabia and Africa was already politically linked before Islam.

events.name: Fall of Himyar
events.source: al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa al-Muluk; Ibn Hisham
events.summary: The Aksumite king Kaleb crossed the Red Sea and ended Himyarite rule in Yemen.
events.context: After the persecution of Najran's Christians, Aksum installed a Christian vassal in Yemen, first Sumyafa Ashwa and then Abraha.
events.significance: Yemen became a Christian Ethiopian dependency; its governor Abraha would later march on Makkah.

events.name: Al-Hira and the Arab Courts
events.summary: Al-Hira, seat of the Lakhmid kings, stood as the Arab court and cultural gateway between the Sasanian empire and the tribes of Arabia in the century before Islam.
events.context: Lakhmid Hira served the Sasanians as a frontier power and became a centre of Arabic poetry, Nestorian Christianity and the Arabic script.
events.significance: The pre-Islamic courts of Hira and Ghassan supplied the political vocabulary and the literacy that the Qur'anic revelation would address.

events.name: Year of the Elephant

quote.arabic: أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصْحَابِ الْفِيلِ
quote.english: Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?

events.summary: Abraha's expedition against Makkah failed in the year tradition remembers as the year of the Prophet's birth.
events.context: Abraha, the Aksumite governor of Yemen, marched north with an elephant; surah al-Fil recalls the destruction of his army before the town.
events.significance: Arabic tradition dated the Prophet's birth to this year, tying his life to a remembered deliverance of Makkah.

events.name: Birth in Makkah
events.summary: Muhammad ibn Abdullah was born in Makkah into the clan of Banu Hashim of Quraysh, in the year remembered as the year of the elephant.
events.context: His father Abdullah had died before his birth and his mother Aminah bint Wahb died when he was six, so he was raised first by his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and then by his uncle Abu Talib.
events.significance: The birth year of 570 CE is the fixed point from which the seerah and the archive's biography of the Prophet ﷺ are dated.

events.name: First Revelation (Surah Al-'Alaq)

quote.english: Read in the name of your Lord who created

events.summary: The first revelation came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the Cave of Hira, marking the beginning of prophethood and of the revelation of the Qur'an.
events.context: Aisha reported that the beginning of revelation was true dreams, and that the Prophet ﷺ used to retreat to the cave of Hira on Jabal al-Nur for seclusion before the angel Jibril brought him the first verses.
events.significance: The event opens the prophetic mission and is the first link of every chain in the archive: all hadith transmission begins from the revelation received here.

events.name: Public Call to Islam
events.summary: The Prophet ﷺ began openly calling the people of Makkah to Islam after three years of secret preaching.
events.context: The first converts included Abu Bakr, Ali, Zayd ibn Harithah and Bilal; with the public call the Quraysh began to organise opposition to the new community.
events.significance: The public call turned a private circle of believers into a visible community, the body of Companions the archive documents.

events.name: Boycott of Banu Hashim
events.summary: Quraysh imposed a social and economic boycott on the Prophet ﷺ and his clan.
events.context: The clans of Quraysh bound themselves by a written pact to cut trade, marriage and social contact with Banu Hashim; the clan withdrew to the valley of Abu Talib for some three years until the pact was torn up.
events.significance: The boycott documents the pressure exerted on the Prophet's clan before the migration, and the cost borne by the community in Makkah.

events.name: Year of Sorrow
events.summary: In the same year the Prophet ﷺ lost his wife Khadijah bint Khuwaylid and his protector Abu Talib.
events.context: Khadijah had been the first believer and had supported the mission from its beginning; Abu Talib's protection had shielded his nephew from Quraysh's worst pressure.
events.significance: The loss of both protections left the Prophet ﷺ exposed in Makkah and preceded the journey to Ta'if and the search for support outside the town.

events.name: Isra and Mi'raj
events.summary: The Prophet ﷺ was taken on a night journey from Makkah to Jerusalem and then to the heavens.
events.context: The journey is recorded in surah al-Isra and in the hadith of the night prayer; Abu Bakr's immediate acceptance of the report is remembered in the tradition.
events.significance: The five daily prayers are dated by the tradition to this night, so the event stands at the head of the archive's prayer records.

events.name: First Pledge of Aqabah
events.summary: A group from Yathrib (Madinah) pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ at Aqabah.
events.context: Twelve men of the Aws and Khazraj met the Prophet ﷺ at the pilgrimage season at Mina and pledged to keep the terms of the first pledge, opening Medinan contact with the mission.
events.significance: The pledge prepared the ground for the migration and gave the community its first organised support outside Makkah.

events.name: Second Pledge of Aqabah
events.summary: A larger group from Yathrib pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ, paving the way for the migration.
events.context: Seventy-three men and two women of Yathrib undertook to defend the Prophet ﷺ as they would their own families, and he appointed twelve representatives among them.
events.significance: The pledge turned Madinah into a place of refuge and made the Hijrah of the following months possible.

events.name: The Hijrah (Migration)

quote.english: Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us

events.summary: The Prophet ﷺ migrated from Makkah to Madinah, marking a new phase in Islamic history.
events.context: After the pledges of Aqabah the Muslims left Makkah in small groups; the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr travelled together by way of the cave of Thawr until they reached Madinah.
events.significance: The year of the migration became year one of the Hijri calendar and the founding moment of the Muslim polity in Madinah.

events.name: Battle of Badr

quote.arabic: وَلَقَدْ نَصَرَكُمُ اللَّهُ بِبَدْرٍ وَأَنتُمْ أَذِلَّةٌ
quote.english: And Allah had certainly assisted you at Badr while you were few in number

events.summary: A decisive victory for the Muslims against the Quraysh, despite being outnumbered.
events.context: The Muslim force of about three hundred met a Quraysh caravan army of roughly a thousand at the wells of Badr; the battle is the first major engagement of the Madinan period.
events.significance: Badr established the military standing of the young polity and is the most frequently cited battle in the Qur'anic and hadith record.

events.name: Battle of Uhud

quote.english: And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you

events.summary: The Muslims met Quraysh again at Uhud, where the battle turned against them after the archers left their position.
events.context: The Prophet ﷺ placed archers on the slope of Uhud to hold the Muslim flank; their withdrawal to gather spoils let Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry, still with Quraysh, attack from the rear.
events.significance: The setback at Uhud is discussed at length in surah Al Imran and shaped the community's later military practice.

events.name: Battle of the Trench

quote.arabic: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اذْكُرُوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ
quote.english: O you who have believed, remember the favour of Allah upon you

events.summary: Madinah was besieged by a confederacy of Quraysh and their allies, and the Muslims held them off behind a defensive trench.
events.context: Salman al-Farsi proposed digging the trench on the exposed northern approaches of Madinah; the siege lasted about a month before the confederacy broke up.
events.significance: The failed siege ended Quraysh's ability to threaten Madinah directly and is recalled in surah al-Ahzab.

events.name: Treaty of Hudaybiyyah

quote.english: Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph

events.summary: A ten-year truce was concluded between the Muslims and Quraysh at Hudaybiyyah.
events.context: The Prophet ﷺ set out for pilgrimage and was halted short of Makkah; Uthman carried the Muslim terms into the town, and the agreement was written with Ali as scribe.
events.significance: The Qur'an calls the truce a clear triumph: it recognised the Muslims as a party to treaty and opened a period of peaceful expansion.

events.name: Battle of Khaybar
events.summary: The Muslim force took the fortified oases of Khaybar north of Madinah.
events.context: Khaybar's fortresses had hosted the confederacy's political organisers after the Trench; the campaign concluded with terms that left the inhabitants on the land as cultivators.
events.significance: The settlement at Khaybar became the model for later agreements with non-Muslim communities under Muslim rule.

events.name: Battle of Mu'tah
events.summary: A Muslim force met Byzantine-allied Arab troops at Mu'tah in the Levant.
events.context: The expedition began as a response to the killing of the envoy al-Harith ibn Umayr; three commanders fell in turn and Khalid ibn al-Walid brought the force back to Madinah.
events.significance: Mu'tah was the first Muslim engagement with the Byzantine sphere and the first campaign in which Khalid ibn al-Walid commanded.

events.name: Conquest of Makkah

quote.english: When the victory of Allah has come and the conquest

events.summary: The Prophet ﷺ entered Makkah with the Muslims and the town accepted Islam.
events.context: Quraysh's allies had broken the truce of Hudaybiyyah; the Muslims marched on Makkah, which was entered with a general amnesty, and Bilal gave the call to prayer at the Ka'ba.
events.significance: The conquest returned the Muslims to the town they had left in 622 and made the Ka'ba the centre of the growing Muslim polity.

events.name: Battle of Hunayn
events.summary: The Muslims defeated the Hawazin and Thaqif tribes in the valley of Hunayn after the conquest of Makkah.
events.context: The tribes had gathered to attack the Muslims soon after the conquest; the Muslim force was thrown into disorder at first and then rallied around the Prophet ﷺ.
events.significance: Hunayn extended Muslim authority over the tribes of the Ta'if hinterland and is addressed in surah al-Tawbah.

events.name: Expedition to Tabuk
events.summary: The largest Muslim expedition of the prophetic period marched north to Tabuk without meeting a Byzantine force.
events.context: Reports of a Byzantine mobilisation in the Levant prompted the campaign; Ali ibn Abi Talib was left in charge of Madinah, and agreements were made with several northern oases on the way.
events.significance: Tabuk marked the northern limit of Muslim campaigning in the Prophet's lifetime and prepared the ground for the later conquests in the Levant.

events.name: Farewell Pilgrimage
events.summary: The Prophet ﷺ performed the pilgrimage with the Muslims and delivered the sermon at Arafat.
events.context: The rites he performed that year became the model of the Hajj, and the sermon at Arafat set out the inviolability of life, property and honour among the believers.
events.significance: The farewell sermon is the archive's central statement of the Prophet's ﷺ final instructions to the community.

events.name: Passing of the Prophet ﷺ
events.summary: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ died in Madinah in the house of Aisha and was buried there.
events.context: He fell ill in the months after the farewell pilgrimage; the community's leadership passed to Abu Bakr, who addressed the Muslims in the mosque on the day of the death.
events.significance: The death closes the prophetic period, ends personal transmission from the Prophet ﷺ, and opens the era of the Companions as the archive's first narrators.

events.name: Ridda Wars
events.summary: The first caliph brought the tribes that had withheld zakah and left Islam back under the authority of Madinah.
events.context: After the death of the Prophet ﷺ several tribes withheld allegiance and zakah; Abu Bakr refused to distinguish between the prayer and the alms and sent eleven columns, with Khalid ibn al-Walid commanding in Yamamah.
events.significance: The wars preserved the unity of the new community and produced the army that carried the conquests into Iraq and the Levant.

events.name: Battle of Yarmuk
events.summary: The Muslim army broke the Byzantine field army at the Yarmuk river in the Levant.
events.context: Khalid ibn al-Walid and Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah commanded Muslim forces that had gathered from the Syrian front; the defeat ended Byzantine rule in Syria.
events.significance: Yarmuk opened the Levant to the caliphate and made Damascus, and later Jerusalem, Muslim-held cities.

events.name: Surrender of Jerusalem
events.summary: Jerusalem came under Muslim rule by agreement, with the caliph Umar receiving the surrender in person.
events.context: After the failure of the Byzantine defence at Yarmuk, the city's leaders negotiated terms; the tradition records that Umar travelled to receive the keys and guaranteed the safety of the inhabitants and their churches.
events.significance: The surrender established a treaty model for the cities of the Levant and gave the Muslims custodianship of the third sanctuary of Islam.

events.name: Garrison Cities of Kufa and Basra
events.summary: The caliphate founded the garrison cities of Basra and Kufa in Iraq to settle the Arab armies.
events.context: Umar directed that the armies should not disperse into the conquered countryside; Basra was laid out in 636 and Kufa shortly after, both becoming centres of Muslim learning and politics.
events.significance: Kufa and Basra became the seats of Ali's caliphate and of the earliest schools of hadith transmission that fill the archive.

events.name: Conquest of Egypt
events.summary: Muslim forces from Syria took Egypt and its capital Alexandria.
events.context: Amr ibn al-As crossed Sinai with the approval of Umar and reduced the Byzantine garrisons; Alexandria fell in 641 and the new settlement of Fustat was founded beside it.
events.significance: Egypt became the caliphate's granary and the base from which the Fatimid, Ayyubid and Mamluk states later ruled.

events.name: Battle of Nihawand
events.summary: The Muslims defeated the last Sasanian field army in the Persian highlands.
events.context: Umar directed the campaign from Madinah; the battle ended organised Sasanian resistance and left the Iranian plateau open to the caliphate.
events.significance: Nihawand is remembered as the opening of the conquest of Persia, whose cities later became the eastern centres of scholarship.

events.name: Standardisation of the Qur'anic Codex
events.summary: The caliph Uthman had the Qur'anic text collected into a single standard codex and copies distributed to the garrison cities.
events.context: The sheets assembled in Abu Bakr's time were held by Hafsa bint Umar; a committee headed by Zayd ibn Thabit produced the standard text, and variant readings in the provinces were withdrawn in its favour.
events.significance: The codex fixed the written text that every hadith and commentary in the archive quotes, and is the earliest event in the archive's transmission history after the revelation itself.

events.name: First Fitna
events.summary: Political conflict over the caliphate opened with the killing of Uthman in Madinah.
events.context: Grievances over provincial administration and the conduct of the conquests brought armed groups to Madinah; Uthman was killed in his house and Ali ibn Abi Talib was recognised as caliph.
events.significance: The fitna divided the community's political leadership and shaped the questions of authority against which later hadith transmission was read.

events.name: Battle of the Camel
events.summary: Forces loyal to Ali met those of Aisha, Talha and al-Zubayr near Basra.
events.context: The three Companions sought redress for Uthman's killing; negotiations failed and fighting broke out, ending with the defeat of the Basran party.
events.significance: The battle was the first armed clash between Muslims over the caliphate, and its memory shapes the narrators' reports of that generation.

events.name: Battle of Siffin
events.summary: Ali's forces and Mu'awiya's Syrian army fought on the Euphrates without a decisive result.
events.context: The confrontation ended in arbitration, which split Ali's own supporters and produced the Kharijite movement.
events.significance: Siffin marks the division of the community into the camps whose later states, Umayyad and otherwise, the Dynasties page records.

events.name: Martyrdom of Ali
events.summary: Ali ibn Abi Talib was killed in Kufa, ending the period of the rightly guided caliphs.
events.context: He had moved the seat of the caliphate to Kufa during the civil war; his son Hasan succeeded briefly before handing authority to Mu'awiya.
events.significance: Ali's death closes the Rashidun caliphate and leads directly into the founding of the Umayyad state in Damascus.

events.name: Damascus Made the Capital
events.summary: Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan was recognised as caliph and ruled from Damascus, founding the Umayyad caliphate.
events.context: After the death of Ali, his son Hasan handed authority to Mu'awiya to end the fighting; the seat of government moved from Iraq and the Hejaz to Syria.
events.significance: Damascus became the centre of a caliphate that stretched from the Atlantic to the Indus within a century.

events.name: Founding of Kairouan
events.summary: The Umayyad governor Uqba ibn Nafi founded Kairouan as the base of Muslim rule in Ifriqiya.
events.context: The new garrison city lay inland from the coast and became the capital of the province of Ifriqiya, from which campaigns pushed westwards across North Africa.
events.significance: Kairouan became the first great centre of Muslim scholarship in North Africa and the base of the later Aghlabid and Fatimid states.

events.name: Battle of Karbala
events.summary: Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of the Prophet ﷺ, was killed at Karbala with his companions by forces of the Umayyad caliph Yazid.
events.context: Husayn had left Makkah for Kufa at the invitation of its supporters, but the Kufan rising had already collapsed and his small party was intercepted in the desert.
events.significance: The killing of the Prophet's ﷺ grandson became the founding event of Shi'i devotion and a permanent reference point in Muslim political memory.

events.name: Dome of the Rock Completed
events.summary: The Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik completed the Dome of the Rock on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem.
events.context: The building was raised above the rock associated with the Prophet's ﷺ night journey, at a time when Abd al-Malik's authority was contested in Iraq.
events.significance: The Dome is among the earliest surviving monumental works of Islamic architecture and shows the caliphate's claim on Jerusalem.

events.name: Abd al-Malik's Administrative Reforms
events.summary: Arabic replaced Greek and Persian in the state registers and a distinct Islamic coinage was struck.
events.context: Abd al-Malik's chancery reform made Arabic the language of administration from Syria to Iraq, and the dinar was minted with Qur'anic legends instead of imperial portraits.
events.significance: The reforms made Arabic the shared written language of the caliphate, the language in which the hadith corpus was recorded.

events.name: Muslim Conquest of Al-Andalus
events.source: Ibn Khaldun, Kitab al-Ibar; al-Maqqari, Nafh al-Tib
events.summary: A Muslim force crossed from North Africa and ended Visigothic rule in the Iberian peninsula.
events.context: Tariq ibn Ziyad landed at Gibraltar in 711 and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic; within a few years most of the peninsula was under Muslim rule and Cordoba became its capital.
events.significance: Al-Andalus carried the caliphate's frontier to western Europe and became a centre of scholarship that fed the archive's later transmission.

events.name: Battle of Tours-Poitiers
events.summary: A Muslim expedition into Frankish territory was turned back between Tours and Poitiers.
events.context: The force had campaigned north from Al-Andalus through Aquitaine; the Frankish mayor of the palace Charles met it on the road and the Muslim army withdrew after the battle.
events.significance: The engagement marked the northern limit of Umayyad expansion in western Europe, and the Pyrenees frontier that followed.

events.name: Umayyad Emirate of Cordoba
events.summary: Abd al-Rahman I, an Umayyad survivor of the Abbasid revolution, established an independent Umayyad emirate in Al-Andalus.
events.context: He crossed from North Africa in 755 and was recognised in Cordoba the following year; the Syrian and Yemeni factions of the peninsula backed him against the existing governor.
events.significance: The Cordoban emirate shows an Umayyad branch ruling on after the dynasty lost the east, so an event's era and its dynasty need not coincide.

events.name: Abbasid Revolution
events.summary: The Abbasid family and its Khurasani supporters overthrew the Umayyad caliphate.
events.context: Abu Muslim raised Khurasan in the name of the Abbasid family from 747; the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II was defeated at the Zab in 750 and the Abbasids were proclaimed at Kufa.
events.significance: The revolution ended Umayyad rule in the east and moved the centre of the caliphate from Syria to Iraq.

events.name: Battle of Talas
events.source: al-Tabari; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh
events.summary: Abbasid forces defeated a Tang Chinese army in the frontier zone of Transoxiana.
events.context: The battle near Talas settled the eastern limit of the caliphate's expansion; paper-making is traditionally said to have travelled west from the craftsmen taken in its aftermath.
events.significance: Transoxiana remained within the Muslim world, and Bukhara and Samarkand became the great centres of hadith scholarship in the following centuries.

events.name: Founding of Baghdad
events.summary: The caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad as the new capital of the Abbasid caliphate.
events.context: The round city was built on the Tigris at the point where the Tigris and Euphrates routes met, close to the old Sasanian capital at Ctesiphon.
events.significance: Baghdad became the political and scholarly centre of the Muslim world, the city in which the great compilations of the archive were assembled.

events.name: Caliphate of Harun al-Rashid
events.summary: Harun al-Rashid ruled the Abbasid caliphate at the height of its wealth and central authority.
events.context: His reign combined campaigns on the Byzantine frontier with the administration of a vast tax-and-trade empire whose revenues were proverbial.
events.significance: The reign marks the peak of the Abbasid caliphate and the classic period of the transmitters of the second and third generations.

events.name: Bayt al-Hikma Established
events.summary: The caliph al-Ma'mun enlarged the House of Wisdom in Baghdad as a library and centre of translation.
events.context: Greek, Persian and Indian works were translated into Arabic under court patronage; the same decades saw the systematic collection and criticism of hadith.
events.significance: Court patronage of translation and scholarship made Baghdad the intellectual centre through which the archive's written tradition passed.

events.name: Samarra Made the Capital
events.summary: The caliph al-Mu'tasim moved the seat of government from Baghdad to the new city of Samarra.
events.context: The move followed friction between the caliph's Turkish troops and the people of Baghdad; for half a century the caliphate ruled from Samarra while Baghdad remained the commercial centre.
events.significance: The move begins the period of military tutelage in which the caliphs' power was increasingly exercised by their commanders.

events.name: Anarchy at Samarra
events.summary: The killing of the caliph al-Mutawakkil began a decade in which four caliphs were raised and deposed by the military.
events.context: The Turkish and other guard regiments in Samarra made and unmade caliphs; provincial governors withheld revenue and dynasties began to rule their provinces in their own name.
events.significance: Central Abbasid authority fragmented from this decade, the political background to the local dynasties of the Dynasties page.

events.name: Founding of Cairo
events.source: Ibn Muyassar, Akhbar Misr; al-Maqrizi, al-Khitat
events.summary: The Fatimids took Egypt and founded Cairo as the capital of their Ismaili caliphate.
events.context: The Fatimid general Jawhar founded al-Qahira beside Fustat in 969 and al-Azhar was established as a centre of learning; the Abbasid name was replaced in the Friday sermon.
events.significance: Cairo became the seat of a rival caliphate claiming descent from the Prophet's ﷺ family, and the city that Fatimid, Ayyubid and Mamluk rule shared.

events.name: Seljuk Entry into Baghdad
events.summary: Tughril Beg entered Baghdad and was recognised as sultan by the Abbasid caliph.
events.context: The Seljuk sultan took the title of protector of the caliph and ended the Buyid domination of the city; the caliph remained as the nominal head of the Sunni community.
events.significance: The arrangement separated the religious authority of the caliph from the military authority of the sultan, a pattern the later sultanates inherited.

events.name: Battle of Manzikert
events.summary: The Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine army and captured its emperor.
events.context: The battle was fought near lake Van in eastern Anatolia; the Byzantine defeat opened the interior of Anatolia to Turkmen settlement.
events.significance: Manzikert transformed the demography of Anatolia and created the frontier on which the Ottoman state later grew.

events.name: Crusader Capture of Jerusalem
events.summary: The army of the First Crusade took Jerusalem from Fatimid rule.
events.context: The Fatimids had recovered the city from the Seljuks the year before; the crusader capture ended four and a half centuries of Muslim rule in Jerusalem until 1187.
events.significance: The loss of Jerusalem shaped the politics of the following century and the careers of the rulers recorded in the Dynasties page.

events.name: Rise of the Ayyubids in Egypt
events.source: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh; Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya
events.summary: Salah al-Din ended the Fatimid caliphate in Egypt and established the Ayyubid sultanate.
events.context: Salah al-Din had come to Egypt as a commander of the Zangid state; on the death of the last Fatimid caliph he had the Friday sermon returned to the Abbasid name and ruled in his own right.
events.significance: The change of dynasty in Cairo transferred the leadership of the Muslim counter-crusade to the Ayyubids.

events.name: Battle of Hattin
events.source: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya
events.summary: Salah al-Din destroyed the army of the kingdom of Jerusalem at the Horns of Hattin.
events.context: The campaign was fought in the heat of July near Tiberias; the defeat of the crusader field army left the coastal towns open and Jerusalem surrendered in the autumn.
events.significance: Hattin restored Jerusalem to Muslim rule and made Salah al-Din the most celebrated ruler of the Ayyubid dynasty.

events.name: Sack of Baghdad
events.source: Ibn Kathir, al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya; Ibn al-Athir
events.summary: The Mongol army of Hulegu took Baghdad and killed the last Abbasid caliph.
events.context: The city fell after a short siege and was plundered for days; libraries and the caliphal treasury were destroyed and the line of caliphs in Baghdad ended.
events.significance: The fall of Baghdad ended the Abbasid caliphate as a political power and is the sharpest break in the political history the archive records.

events.name: Battle of Ayn Jalut
events.summary: The Mamluks of Egypt defeated a Mongol army in Palestine, the first major check to Mongol expansion westward.
events.context: Qutuz and Baybars met the force of Kitbuqa in the Jezreel valley two years after the fall of Baghdad; the victory secured Egypt and Syria for the Mamluk sultanate.
events.significance: Ayn Jalut established the Mamluk sultanate as the leading Muslim power of the time and the protector of the remaining caliphal title in Cairo.

events.name: Fall of Acre
events.source: Ibn Kathir, al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya; Abu al-Fida, al-Mukhtasar fi Akhbar al-Bashar
events.summary: The Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil took Acre, ending the crusader states on the Levantine coast.
events.context: Acre was the last major Latin stronghold; its surrender in 1291 was followed by the evacuation of the remaining coastal towns.
events.significance: The Mamluk sultanate emerged as the undisputed power of Egypt and Syria after two centuries of crusading.

events.name: Foundation of the Ottoman State
events.summary: Osman ibn Ertugrul began to rule independently in the frontier zone of north-western Anatolia.
events.context: The Ottoman beylik grew out of the Seljuk successor frontier facing Byzantine Bithynia; its chronicles place the beginning of Osman's independent rule at 1299.
events.significance: The frontier principality became the longest-lived dynasty of the Muslim world, ruling until 1922.

events.name: Bursa Becomes the Ottoman Capital
events.summary: Orhan took Bursa and made it the first Ottoman capital.
events.context: The capture of the Byzantine city gave the beylik a mint, a market and an administration; the first Ottoman madrasa and mosques were built there.
events.significance: Bursa marks the passage of the Ottoman house from a frontier warband to a settled state.

events.name: Battle of Kosovo
events.summary: The Ottomans defeated a Serbian-led coalition on the Kosovo field.
events.context: Sultan Murad I was killed in or after the battle and was succeeded by Bayezid I; the victory opened the Balkans to Ottoman expansion.
events.significance: Kosovo established Ottoman power south of the Danube and is remembered as the founding battle of Ottoman rule in the Balkans.

events.name: Conquest of Constantinople
events.source: Tursun Beg, Tarikh-i Abu al-Fath; Kritovoulos, History of Mehmed the Conqueror
events.summary: Sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople after a fifty-three day siege.
events.context: The Ottomans used siege cannon against the land walls and moved galleys overland into the Golden Horn; the city became the Ottoman capital and was repopulated by decree.
events.significance: The conquest ended the Byzantine empire and made the Ottoman sultanate the major power of the eastern Mediterranean.

events.name: Fall of Granada
events.summary: Granada surrendered to the armies of Castile and Aragon, ending Muslim rule in the Iberian peninsula.
events.context: The Nasrid emirate was the last Muslim state in Al-Andalus; its surrender in January 1492 followed a decade of war and the union of the Castilian and Aragonese crowns.
events.significance: The event closes eight centuries of Muslim rule in western Europe and stands outside the dynasties of the catalog: the Nasrid emirate is not recorded in the archive.

events.name: Foundation of the Safavid State
events.source: Iskandar Beg Munshi, Tarikh-i Alam-ara-yi Abbasi
events.summary: Isma'il I took Tabriz and was proclaimed shah, founding the Safavid state.
events.context: The Safavid order of Ardabil had gathered Turkmen followers; Isma'il's proclamation was followed by the establishment of Twelver Shi'ism as the religion of the state.
events.significance: The Safavid state fixed a distinct Persian political and religious identity for the following centuries.

events.name: Ottoman Conquest of Mamluk Egypt
events.source: Ibn Iyas, Bada'i al-Zuhur; Ottoman chronicles
events.summary: Selim I defeated the Mamluk sultanate and annexed Egypt and Syria to the Ottoman empire.
events.context: The campaign followed the Ottoman-Mamluk rivalry over the frontier of Anatolia and Syria; the last Mamluk sultan was killed and the Abbasid caliph in Cairo was taken to Istanbul.
events.significance: The conquest ended the Mamluk sultanate, made the Ottomans masters of the eastern Mediterranean and transferred the caliphal title to Istanbul.

events.name: First Battle of Panipat
events.summary: Babur defeated the Lodi sultan of Delhi and founded the Mughal empire.
events.context: Babur had lost his Central Asian heritage and taken Kabul; at Panipat he used field artillery and the tulughma flanking tactic against a much larger Lodi army.
events.significance: The battle transferred north India to the Timurid dynasty that ruled until 1857.

events.name: Siege of Vienna
events.summary: The Ottoman siege of Vienna failed after a relief army broke the besieging force.
events.context: Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha besieged the city from July 1683; the relief army of the Holy Roman Empire and Poland attacked in September and the Ottoman army withdrew.
events.significance: The defeat opened the long retreat of Ottoman power in central Europe, confirmed by the treaty of Karlowitz in 1699.

events.name: French Expedition to Egypt
events.source: al-Jabarti, Aja'ib al-Athar fi al-Tarajim wa al-Akhbar
events.summary: Napoleon's army landed in Egypt and occupied Cairo, ending effective Mamluk power in the province.
events.context: The expedition defeated the Mamluk cavalry at the pyramids and held Cairo until 1801; the Ottoman governor Muhammad Ali later established his own dynasty in the province.
events.significance: The occupation exposed the military and administrative gap between the Ottoman provinces and industrial Europe, and began the century of reform.

events.name: End of the Mughal Empire
events.summary: After the uprising of 1857 the last Mughal emperor was deposed and the dynasty abolished.
events.context: The emperor Bahadur Shah II had been proclaimed leader of the revolt in Delhi; the British retook the city in September 1857, tried him and exiled him to Rangoon, where he died in 1862.
events.significance: The end of the Mughal line closed the last Muslim imperial dynasty of South Asia and transferred sovereignty to the British crown.

events.name: Abolition of the Caliphate
events.source: Turkish Grand National Assembly records, 3 March 1924
events.summary: The Turkish republic abolished the caliphate two years after the sultanate had been ended.
events.context: The Ottoman sultanate was abolished in November 1922 and the last sultan left Istanbul; in March 1924 the assembly abolished the caliphate and exiled the Ottoman family.
events.significance: The abolition ended the institution of the caliphate that had passed from Madinah to Damascus, Baghdad, Cairo and Istanbul, closing the political line this catalog traces.
